answer.label: Not Winston Churchill — actually Ed Greenwood
answer.authorDates: b. 1959 · Canadian fantasy author, creator of the Forgotten Realms
answer.sourceLine: There is no record of Winston Churchill saying or writing this — his quotation editor Richard Langworth files it among the “Red Herrings.” The earliest close match Quote Investigator found ↗ is in Ed Greenwood’s 1993 Forgotten Realms novel The Code of the Harpers — “Ye have enemies? Good, good — that means ye’ve stood up for something” — and Greenwood has said the wording is his, though the sentiment is old. The Churchill credit surfaced only in 2002.

source.heading: Where the line actually comes from
source.excerpt: “Ye have enemies? Good, good — that means ye’ve stood up for something, sometime in thy life…”
trail: Quote Investigator ↗ finds no evidence for Churchill and identifies Ed Greenwood’s 1993 The Code of the Harpers as the earliest close match; Greenwood confirmed “that wording is mine.”
The International Churchill Society ↗ lists this line among quotes falsely attributed to Churchill.
PolitiFact ↗ notes the Churchill version is a rough paraphrase of a sentiment expressed by Victor Hugo a century earlier.
source.excerptNote: The archaic wording as Ed Greenwood gave it to the wizard Elminster in The Code of the Harpers (1993); the smoothed “You have enemies? Good…” version circulated later and was pinned on Churchill.
source.rightsHolder: Ed Greenwood / Wizards of the Coast (formerly TSR)
source.rightsNote: The closest documented wording originates in Ed Greenwood’s novel The Code of the Harpers, first published by TSR in 1993 and therefore in copyright in the United States. The popular smoothed phrasing has no earlier sourced origin, so no public-domain claim can be made.

author.bio: Ed Greenwood (born 1959) is a Canadian fantasy author and game designer best known for creating the Forgotten Realms, the campaign setting used in Dungeons & Dragons. His wizard character Elminster delivers many aphoristic lines across his novels — including, in 1993’s The Code of the Harpers, the earliest close match to this “enemies” quotation. Greenwood has said the sentiment came from his grandfather but the specific wording is his own.

misattribution.heading: How Churchill got the credit
misattribution.intro: This is a feel-good line pinned on Churchill with no source behind it. The trail runs the other way: a fantasy novel supplied the wording, and older writers supplied the idea.

items.why: Churchill died in 1965; the credit first appears in 2002 (in remarks by U.S. Senator Jim Bunning), and no line resembling this is found anywhere in Churchill’s canon. His quotation editor Richard Langworth files it as a “Red Herring,” per Quote Investigator ↗.
The earliest close match is Greenwood’s 1993 novel The Code of the Harpers; Greenwood publicly confirmed “that wording is mine,” via Quote Investigator ↗.

Hugo (1845) and Jefferson (1782) both wrote that having enemies is a mark of having achieved or stood for something — the same idea, in their own very different words, per PolitiFact ↗ and Quote Investigator ↗.

misattribution.truthLine: The idea is old (Hugo, Jefferson); the exact modern wording is Ed Greenwood’s from a 1993 fantasy novel — and Churchill has nothing to do with either, per the International Churchill Society ↗.

context.heading: Why this one sticks to Churchill
lead: Churchill is one of the internet’s biggest magnets for orphaned quotations: a punchy, defiant, morale-boosting line simply sounds like him, so it gets his name whether he said it or not. This “enemies” aphorism fits the pattern perfectly — combative, encouraging, and endlessly shareable.

In reality the words were written for a wizard in a Dungeons & Dragons tie-in novel, then smoothed and reassigned. The sentiment behind them is genuinely old, reaching back through Victor Hugo to Thomas Jefferson — which is why it feels timeless even though the phrasing is barely thirty years old.
context.pull: The idea is centuries old. The wording is from a 1993 fantasy novel. Churchill said neither.
